analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to keep accurate doctor directories and cover costs when listings are wrong.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, despite bipartisan sponsorship.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage is the private-insurance alternative to traditional Medicare, and tens of millions of seniors are enrolled. This bill would require those insurers to publish accurate online directories of in-network doctors, verify each listing at least every 90 days, and remove doctors who leave the network within 5 business days. If a beneficiary picks a doctor the plan's directory wrongly lists as in-network, the plan could only charge in-network cost-sharing — not the much higher out-of-network price. Plans would also have to test and report their directory accuracy each year, with scores posted publicly, and the Government Accountability Office would report to Congress on how it all worked by January 2031.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors in Medicare Advantage network plans. Today, if a plan's directory says a doctor is in-network and the patient books an appointment, but the doctor has actually left the network, the patient can be billed a large out-of-network share of the cost. The bill shifts that cost to the insurer, and forces plans to keep their listings current, accurate, and useful — including flagging whether a doctor is accepting new patients, has disability accommodations, or offers telehealth.

how_it_helps.text: If a beneficiary is treated by a doctor the plan's directory wrongly lists as in-network on the date the appointment was made, the plan must charge only in-network cost sharing [S3].

Plans must maintain an accurate public provider directory, verify every provider's information at least every 90 days, flag unverified listings, and remove departed providers within 5 business days, starting with plan year 2026 [S3].

Directories must include details patients need to actually use the network: whether a provider is accepting new patients, disability accommodations, language capabilities, and telehealth availability [S3].

Plans must annually analyze and report directory accuracy — with special attention to specialties with high error rates like mental health and substance use treatment — and accuracy scores must be posted publicly from 2027, so beneficiaries can compare plans before enrolling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, which bear the cost of verifying thousands of provider listings every 90 days, running annual accuracy analyses, and eating the bill for out-of-network charges caused by their own directory errors. Doctors and hospitals also face some extra work responding to verification requests.

drawbacks.text: The verification schedule is demanding: confirming every provider's status at least every 90 days is a real administrative burden for plans and for the doctors' offices that have to respond to the checks, and plans warned in the bill's own design that burden reduction should be considered [S3].
Insurers could pass compliance costs into Medicare Advantage premiums or benefit design, so some of the protection could come back to beneficiaries as higher costs [S3].
Plans with low enrollment can be waived from the accuracy-reporting requirement at the Secretary's discretion, leaving a gap in coverage for the smallest plans [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is well-targeted: it makes the insurer pay for errors in its own directory rather than the patient, which is hard to object to in principle. The main honest concern is administrative cost — 90-day verification of entire networks is expensive, and some of that cost would likely show up in premiums. The bill tries to soften that with a stakeholder process on data standardization and discretion for the Secretary, but the burden issue is real.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees for its entire life — introduced in March 2024, referred again to a Health Subcommittee in December 2024 — and neither committee ever held a hearing or voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Panetta introduced the bill on March 15, 2024, joined by four cosponsors split evenly between the parties: Reps. Murphy and Fitzpatrick (Republicans) and Kuster and Schneider (Democrats) [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee — the two panels that share jurisdiction over Medicare [S5].
It was referred to the Health Subcommittee on March 22, 2024, and referred to a Health Subcommittee again on December 17, 2024, near the end of the session [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers came out ahead: they avoided the compliance costs of 90-day directory verification and the new liability for charging patients out-of-network rates after their own directories were wrong. Beneficiaries who get surprise bills from directory errors gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — two Republicans and two Democrats joined the Democratic sponsor — but because no committee or floor vote ever happened, no recorded opposition or vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill imposes new costs on MA plans — verifying every provider listing at least every 90 days, annual accuracy audits, and paying in-network rates when their own directory errors stick patients with out-of-network bills. Directory inaccuracy is a known driver of surprise billing for seniors, so the industry's interest in avoiding these rules runs directly against beneficiaries' interest in accurate listings.

Providers bear some added work responding to plan verification requests every 90 days. But they benefit from being listed accurately — a wrong listing means patients who book appointments they cannot serve and revenue disputes with plans — so their interest largely runs alongside patients'.
